title: landing contrast pitches - three-act narrative and hero candidates
content:
Purpose
---
Draft a small battery of landing/hero alternatives that: (a) surface the specific economic + reliability problems we solve for engineering teams, (b) quickly map to product pillars (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private, Optimize, Console), and (c) make simple A/B test permutations for headline + subhead + CTA + one-sentence proof. This doc is intentionally lightweight — brainstorming + rationale + quick QA checklist for experiments.

Audience
---
Primary: software engineers & ML engineers evaluating inference options for production applications. Secondary: platform/infra leads who influence procurement and architecture.

Core positioning we want to test
---
- Primary claim: inference should be predictable and economical. You shouldn’t trade reliability for cost or vice-versa.
- Functional pillars to call out in various variants: predictable latency (SLOs), cost controls (batching, quantization, routing), multi-environment parity (hosted | dedicated | private), and operational guardrails (rollouts, tracing, fallback).

Three-act landing narrative (fast path for copywriters)
---
Act 1 — The tension (problem): "Models exist, predictable serving doesn't." Short lead: “Great models, terrible operational economics.” Bullets for page: unpredictable throughput, token bill surprises, quiet regressions after model changes, regional capacity failures.
Act 2 — The shift (why Redwood): "We decouple model capability from serving economics." Lead: “Same model, reliably cheaper and faster in production.” Quick product mapping: Hosted for fast tests, Dedicated for predictable commits, Private for regulated deployments.
Act 3 — The proof & call to action: measurable unit economics, latency SLOs, customer example snippet + invite (start free / request demo / run a perf test).

Hero candidates (7 rapid variants) with micro-rationale and suggested subhead
---
1) "Predictable inference. Predictable costs."
   Subhead: "Ship LLM features with latency SLOs, cost controls, and a single API across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments."
   Rationale: direct promise about predictability; good for platform leads.

2) "Stop baking serving into your model roadmap."
   Subhead: "Focus on prompts and products — we handle the runtime, routing, and economics at scale."
   Rationale: speaks to engineering time-savings; slightly cheeky.

3) "Same model. Better economics."
   Subhead: "Automatic batching, KV/prefix caching, and smart routing that lower per-token cost without retraining."
   Rationale: technical appeal; calls out optimizations.

4) "Inference that behaves like your app."
   Subhead: "Latency SLOs, fallbacks, and transparent routing policies so customers never see a capacity blip."
   Rationale: reliability-focused; good for customer-facing product pages.

5) "Control latency and cost — not tradeoffs."
   Subhead: "Mix of dedicated pools, quantized model variants, and autoscale policies to hit both SLAs and unit economics."
   Rationale: highlights tradeoff resolution.

6) "From prototype to production without rewriting infra."
   Subhead: "One API, multiple deployment modes, and rollout tools so you can ship guardrails alongside features."
   Rationale: onboarding-focused; good for PLG funnel.

7) "Enterprise-ready inference — without the forklift."
   Subhead: "Private control plane, KMS integrations, and audited logs for regulated workloads."
   Rationale: enterprise compliance angle.

Suggested micro-CTAs (pick one per hero variant)
---
- Start free (developer sandbox)
- Run a latency & cost trial (automated perf scan for your prompt set)
- Request a Dedicated sizing call
- Try a private demo (VPC/on-prem)

Single-line proof snippets to pair with heroes (keep to ~12–16 words)
---
- "25–60% lower per-token cost vs unmanaged self-hosting in customer workloads."
- "99.9% of production requests served within configured SLO during our last QPS test."
- "Customers reduce median inference latency by 35% using autoscale + smart routing."

Layout/flow experiments for homepage top fold (three quick layouts)
---
A. Technical-first: hero + three stacked microcards (Latency SLOs | Cost controls | Multi-mode parity). CTA: "Run your trial". Good for dev-savvy visitors.
B. Narrative-first: short 3-line story (problem -> Redwood shift -> proof) + customer quote + CTA: "See the economics". Good for PMs and buyer journeys.
C. Action-first: hero + immediate input box (enter prompt or upload sample) -> run a short perf/cost preview (mock) + CTA: "Get my report". High friction but high signal.

Competitive notes (quick heuristics for messaging differentiation)
---
- Generic cloud AI endpoints (big clouds): call out that they expose VM capacity & endpoint primitives but don’t provide tight unit-cost controls, automatic KV/prefix caching, or optimized quantization suggestions. Messaging angle: "We bring inference economics, not just endpoints."
- LLM API-first providers (simplicity-focused): they sell speed-to-prototype; highlight Redwood adds production controls (SLOs, rollouts, dedicated pools) and parity across private deployments. Angle: "You can start simple and grow to enterprise-grade without lock-in."
- Self-host inference stacks: win argument is integration & operational burden. Emphasize time-to-value and observability (token-level cost breakdowns, tracing hooks) and auto-fallbacks that reduce on-call burden.
- Specialty inference runtimes (open-source projects): they win on deep customization; Redwood's counter is productization + orchestration + support (dedicated capacity contracts, SLA).

Top competitive battleground messages to test A/B
---
- "Cost-first" variant: emphasize quant metrics and savings.
- "Reliability-first" variant: emphasize SLOs, fallbacks, and multi-region failover.
- "Control-first" variant: emphasize Private + Dedicated + KMS.

Questions we need engineering/product to confirm before experiments
---
- Real % ranges for “typical cost reduction” by workload class (generation vs embeddings) — ask Applied ML for benchmark table (Jira: GT-ops-210).
- Recent P99/P95 latency SLO numbers across hosted vs dedicated for 512-token workloads.
- Which customer logos are safe for public one-liners? (ask Customer Success).

Quick checklist for running the top-fold A/B tests
---
- Create 3 hero variants (Cost-first, Reliability-first, Control-first) in LaunchDarkly for 50/50 split (Dev funnel).
- Hook analytics: measure (a) CTA click-through, (b) time to sign-up, (c) trial-performance tool engagement.
- Run for 2 weeks, ensure traffic cohort parity by referrer and company size.

Rough copy fragments for lower-funnel product page sections
---
- Feature header: "Predictable runtime, fewer surprises" -> body: "Autoscaling pools, fallback routing, and token-level cost attribution so you can forecast spend and performance."
- Feature header: "Optimize: recommendations that reduce costs without regressions" -> body: "Automated quantization profiles and batching suggestions tuned to your prompt distribution."
- Feature header: "Rollouts & safe upgrades" -> body: "Canary routes, automatic fallback to earlier model variants, and traceable rollouts that catch regressions before they affect customers."

Notes-to-self / open brainstorm fragments (messy, keep)
---
- Try a micro-experiment where the hero CTA is "Run your prompt" and returns a 3-line preview + estimated cost (very high signal for devs).
- Consider a tiny interactive showing how batching + KV cache reduces cost on a 10k-user/day use case.
- For enterprise audiences, create a variant where the hero is a short customer quote: "Saved 43% on inference costs in 30 days — SRE lead, fintech" (placeholder until legal signoff).

Next steps / owners
---
- Ask Applied ML for benchmark table and short explanation of quantization/kv benefits (owner: Marta Lee, due: 2025-11-24).
- Engineering to confirm SLO numbers & feasible demo for "run your prompt" (owner: Jordan Patel, due: 2025-11-27).
- Copy team to produce 3 tightened hero options and submit to A/B infra (owner: Ben Rodriguez, due: 2025-12-02).

Last quick takeaways
---
Keep top-fold copy tightly about developer economics and reliability. Test direct numeric claims vs qualitative reassurance (SLOs, fallbacks). The winning creative is likely to be the one that gives an immediate sense of operational safety (latency/cost predictability) while offering a low-effort way to validate on your own prompts.
